faq.q: Is the Armenian alphabet hard to learn?
faq.a: Not really — it has 39 letters and, unlike English, each letter almost always makes exactly one sound. Once you've drilled the sounds, reading Armenian is far more predictable than reading English.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn the Armenian alphabet?
faq.a: Most learners can recognize and sound out every letter within one to two weeks of short daily practice — Haylingua's own alphabet course is broken into 11 bite-sized lessons for exactly this pace.

faq.q: What's the difference between Eastern and Western Armenian letters?
faq.a: The letterforms and alphabet order are identical — the difference is in pronunciation of certain letter pairs. Haylingua teaches Standard Eastern Armenian, the form used in Armenia today.

faq.q: Do I need to learn cursive Armenian handwriting?
faq.a: Not to read or type Armenian — the printed letterforms shown on this page are what you'll see everywhere online and in most print. Handwriting is a separate, optional skill you can pick up later.

meta.title: Armenian Pronunciation Guide: How to Pronounce Armenian
meta.description: Learn how to pronounce Armenian correctly with real native audio. Master aspirated vs. unaspirated consonants, both Armenian R sounds, and tricky letters with no English equivalent.

hero.title: Armenian Pronunciation
hero.subtitle: Armenian is almost entirely phonetic — once you know a letter's sound, it's the same in every word. The hard part isn't the rules, it's a handful of sounds English speakers haven't trained their mouths to make. Here's what to listen for, with real audio.

trickyPairs.title: Unaspirated vs. aspirated stops
trickyPairs.text: Armenian distinguishes a plain, no-breath consonant from the same consonant said with a burst of air — a contrast English doesn't make. Compare a crisp «տ» (t) with a puffed-out «թ» (t').

trickyPairs.title: Two kinds of R
trickyPairs.text: Eastern Armenian has a light single tongue-tap «ր» (close to the American 'tt' in 'butter') and a strongly rolled/trilled «ռ» — mixing them up is one of the most common beginner errors.

trickyPairs.title: Sounds with no English equivalent
trickyPairs.text: A few Armenian consonants don't map onto anything in English at all — «խ» is a rasping throat sound like the Scottish 'ch' in loch, and «ղ» is a soft, gargled sound close to a French 'r'.

hero.title: Eastern Armenian
hero.subtitle: Armenian has two living literary standards — Eastern and Western. Eastern Armenian is the official language of the Republic of Armenia today, and it's what Haylingua teaches.

easternArmenian.note: The two share the same 39-letter alphabet and a large amount of vocabulary and grammar — the biggest practical difference for a beginner is pronunciation, especially of the plain vs. puffed-out consonant pairs (see the {{link}}).

faq.q: Is Eastern or Western Armenian more useful to learn?
faq.a: It depends on who you'll speak with. Eastern Armenian is the official language of the Republic of Armenia and is spoken by the majority of Armenian speakers worldwide. Western Armenian is more common among diaspora communities with roots in the Ottoman Empire — parts of the U.S., France, and the Middle East.

faq.q: Can an Eastern Armenian speaker understand Western Armenian?
faq.a: Largely yes, with practice — the two are close enough that speakers can often follow each other, similar to the relationship between some closely related Romance languages. Vocabulary, some grammar, and especially pronunciation differ enough to cause real confusion at first.

faq.q: Does Haylingua teach Western Armenian too?
faq.a: Not yet — Haylingua's course teaches Standard Eastern Armenian. It's a natural foundation even if your family speaks Western Armenian, since the alphabet and a large share of vocabulary and grammar overlap.

meta.title: Armenian Numbers 1–100: Count in Armenian With Pronunciation
meta.description: Learn Armenian numbers from 1 to 100 with Armenian script and pronunciation for every number, plus how compound numbers and ordinals are built.

hero.title: Armenian Numbers 1–100
hero.subtitle: Every number you need for prices, ages, dates, and phone numbers — in Armenian script, with pronunciation for each one.

armenianNumbers.compoundsNote: Past twenty, Armenian stacks the ten and the ones digit into a single word — no extra connector, no hyphen. Twenty-five is քսանհինգ (k'san-hing), literally "twenty-five" run together. Once you know the ten words above and the digits 1–9, you can build every number up to 99 without learning anything new.
armenianNumbers.ordinalsNote: Ordinals are formed from the cardinal number, mostly with the ending -երորդ (-erord). The first three are irregular and worth memorising as-is; everything from fourth onward follows the pattern.

faq.q: Are Armenian numbers hard to learn?
faq.a: They're one of the easier parts of the language. The digits 1–10 are short, the teens are transparent compounds of "ten" plus the digit, and everything above twenty follows one predictable stacking rule. Most learners are comfortable counting to 100 within a few days.

faq.q: Does Armenian use the same digits as English?
faq.a: Yes — modern Armenian writes numerals with the same 0–9 Arabic digits you already use, so prices, phone numbers, and dates are readable straight away. There is also a historical Armenian numeral system that uses letters of the alphabet, but you'll only meet it in old manuscripts and on monuments, not in everyday life.

faq.q: Are these numbers Eastern or Western Armenian?
faq.a: The words on this page are Standard Eastern Armenian, the form spoken in Armenia today. Western Armenian uses the same number words, but pronounces several consonants differently — for example the initial sounds shift, so the same spelling is voiced differently. See our Western vs Eastern Armenian comparison for the full picture.

faq.q: How do I say a year or a phone number in Armenian?
faq.a: Years are read as a full number (հազար ինը հարյուր… for 19xx), while phone numbers are usually read digit by digit, exactly as in English. Both only require the 0–100 vocabulary on this page plus հազար (ha-zar, thousand).

armenianPhrases.politenessNote: Armenian has a formal and an informal "you", and travelers are safest defaulting to the formal one (դուք, duk') with anyone they haven't been introduced to. The phrases above already use the polite forms, so you can say them to a stranger without a second thought.

faq.q: Do I need Armenian to travel in Armenia?
faq.a: You can get by without it — Russian is widely understood and English is common among younger people and in Yerevan's tourist areas. But even a handful of Armenian phrases changes how people respond to you, especially outside the capital, and it's genuinely appreciated rather than treated as a novelty.

faq.q: Which Armenian should I learn for travel to Armenia?
faq.a: Eastern Armenian. That's what's spoken in Armenia itself, and it's what every phrase on this page uses. Western Armenian is the diaspora variety — invaluable if you're connecting with family in Lebanon, Los Angeles, or Europe, but not what you'll hear in Yerevan.

faq.q: Will people understand me if my pronunciation is imperfect?
faq.a: Almost always, yes. The sounds most likely to trip you up are the aspirated consonants — the difference between a plain and a "puffed" p, t, or k can change a word, but context usually carries you through. Listening to real audio while you learn matters far more than drilling the script silently.

faq.q: Is Armenian written in its own alphabet?
faq.a: Yes — 39 letters, created around 405 AD, unrelated to Latin or Cyrillic. Street signs and menus in Armenia are largely in Armenian script, often alongside English in tourist areas. Learning to read it takes a few days and makes navigating dramatically easier.

meta.title: Western vs Eastern Armenian: Differences & Which to Learn
meta.description: Western and Eastern Armenian compared — where each is spoken, how pronunciation and spelling differ, how mutually intelligible they are, and which one you should learn.

hero.title: Western vs Eastern Armenian
hero.subtitle: Two standard forms of the same language, shaped by very different histories. Here's how they actually differ — and how to decide which one to learn.

westernVsEastern.intro: Armenian split into two written standards in the nineteenth century, along the border between the Ottoman and Russian empires. Eastern Armenian became the language of what is now the Republic of Armenia; Western Armenian became the language of the communities that were scattered across the world after 1915. They share an alphabet, most of their vocabulary, and their grammar's underlying shape — speakers of one can generally follow the other after a short adjustment, the way a Lisbon and a São Paulo speaker manage Portuguese.

comparisonRows.western: The global diaspora — Lebanon, Syria, France, the US, Argentina

comparisonRows.eastern: Several million, with a national state behind it
comparisonRows.western: Fewer, and classified by UNESCO as endangered

comparisonRows.eastern: Official language of the Republic of Armenia
comparisonRows.western: No state; sustained by diaspora schools, churches, and press

comparisonRows.eastern: Present tense built with the participle plus "to be"
comparisonRows.western: Present tense marked with the prefix կը (gə)

comparisonRows.eastern: Travel to Armenia, business, most online resources
comparisonRows.western: Connecting with diaspora family and heritage communities

westernVsEastern.soundShiftHeading: The sound shift, in one rule
westernVsEastern.soundShift: The difference you'll notice first is a consistent swap in how certain consonants are voiced. Where Eastern Armenian says a voiced b, d, or g, Western Armenian typically says an unvoiced p, t, or k — and vice versa. The spelling stays identical; only the pronunciation moves. Once you internalise this single correspondence, a surprising amount of the other variety becomes readable to you immediately.
westernVsEastern.whichToLearnHeading: So which one should you learn?
westernVsEastern.whichToLearnIntro: There's no universally better answer — it depends entirely on why you're learning. In practice:
whichToLearnPoints: Learn **Eastern** if you're travelling to, working with, or moving to Armenia, or if you simply want the variety with the most learning material, media, and everyday online use.
Learn **Western** if your family is from the diaspora and Western Armenian is what your grandparents spoke — that connection is the whole point, and it's the variety at genuine risk of being lost.
If you have no particular tie either way, Eastern is the more practical starting point, and what you learn transfers substantially if you later pick up Western.
westernVsEastern.whatWeTeach: Haylingua teaches Standard Eastern Armenian — the form spoken in Armenia today. If your goal is Western Armenian specifically, we'd rather tell you that plainly up front than have you discover it three lessons in. Much of the alphabet and vocabulary work still transfers, but the pronunciation and verb forms you'll hear here are Eastern.

faq.q: Can Eastern and Western Armenian speakers understand each other?
faq.a: Largely, yes. The two are mutually intelligible for most everyday purposes, though the first conversation takes some adjustment — the consonant shift and a handful of high-frequency verb forms are what cause the initial friction. Written Armenian is easier to cross over than spoken, since the alphabet is shared.

faq.q: Do they use the same alphabet?
faq.a: Yes, the same 39-letter Armenian alphabet. The difference is spelling convention: Eastern Armenian adopted a spelling reform in the Soviet period, while Western Armenian kept the classical orthography. Some words are therefore spelled differently even though the letters are identical.

faq.q: Which one is 'real' or 'original' Armenian?
faq.a: Neither, and it's worth pushing back on the premise. Both descend from Classical Armenian (Grabar) and both are legitimate modern standards with their own literature. Western Armenian preserves the older spelling; Eastern Armenian has the larger living speaker base. Neither is a corruption of the other.

faq.q: Is Western Armenian dying out?
faq.a: It's genuinely endangered — UNESCO classifies it as such — because it has no state backing it and is transmitted mainly through diaspora families and schools. That's precisely why heritage learners choosing Western Armenian are doing something valuable, even though it's the harder path for finding resources.

meta.title: How to Choose an Armenian Learning App (2026 Guide)
meta.description: What actually matters when picking an app to learn Armenian — alphabet coverage, real audio, Eastern vs Western, and the questions worth asking before you commit.

hero.title: How to choose an Armenian learning app
hero.subtitle: Armenian is served by far fewer tools than Spanish or French, and the ones that exist differ in ways that matter. Here's what to check before you commit your time.

choosingAnApp.disclosure: Straight up: Haylingua is our own app, so treat this as an informed argument rather than a neutral review. We've written the criteria below to be useful even if you decide something else fits you better — and we'll tell you plainly where we're not the right answer.

criteria.title: Does it teach the alphabet properly?
criteria.text: Armenian has its own 39-letter script, unrelated to Latin or Cyrillic. An app that transliterates everything into Latin letters lets you start faster but leaves you unable to read a menu, a street sign, or a message from a relative. Check that the script is taught from the first lesson, not bolted on later as an optional extra.

criteria.title: Is there real audio on every word?
criteria.text: Armenian distinguishes plain from aspirated consonants — the difference between a plain and a "puffed" p, t, or k is meaningful, and it's nearly impossible to acquire from text alone. A handful of sample recordings isn't enough. You want audio attached to every item you're asked to learn.

criteria.title: Eastern or Western Armenian?
criteria.text: This is the single most consequential question, and many tools don't state it clearly. Eastern is spoken in Armenia; Western is the diaspora variety. Learning the wrong one for your goal is a genuinely costly mistake, so find the answer before your first lesson — see our full comparison if you're unsure which you want.

criteria.title: Was it built for Armenian, or ported to it?
criteria.text: Apps that cover dozens of languages from one template tend to treat Armenian's specifics — its sound system, its script, its verb formation — as an afterthought. A tool built for Armenian alone can structure the whole curriculum around the things that actually make it hard.

criteria.title: Can you actually sustain it?
criteria.text: The best app is the one you still open in week six. Short lessons, a visible streak, and immediate feedback matter more than an exhaustive syllabus you abandon. Be honest about whether a tool fits ten minutes on a commute or assumes an hour at a desk.

criteria.title: What does it cost to find out?
criteria.text: Armenian tools vary from free to subscription-only. A meaningful free tier lets you get through the alphabet and judge the teaching quality before paying for anything — which is the only reliable way to evaluate any of this.

faq.q: Is Armenian on Duolingo?
faq.a: No — Duolingo has never offered an Armenian course, and it remains one of the most commonly searched disappointments for new Armenian learners. If you arrived here after searching for it, you'll need to look at Armenian-specific or smaller multi-language tools instead.

faq.q: Can I learn Armenian free?
faq.a: Yes, at least to a real foundation. Haylingua is free to start with no card required, and there are also free community resources, YouTube channels, and Anki decks. Paid tutoring becomes genuinely valuable later, once you have enough language to make conversation practice worthwhile.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn Armenian?
faq.a: The alphabet takes most learners under a week. Basic conversational footing — greetings, numbers, ordering, simple questions — is a matter of a few months of consistent short sessions. Fluency, as with any language, is measured in years, and depends far more on regular contact with the language than on which app you picked.

faq.q: Is Armenian hard for English speakers?
faq.a: It's moderately hard: a new script, a case system, and some unfamiliar consonant distinctions. But the script is phonetic and learnable in days, and Armenian spelling is far more consistent than English. The difficulty is mostly front-loaded, which is why the first two weeks matter so much.
